evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: Sex Differences in Diagnostic Delay, Misdiagnosis, and Disability in Persistent Lyme Disease (MyLymeData)
spec.boundary: This simulator models self-reported percentage-point differences between women and men in a single self-selected patient registry (MyLymeData, n=2170, dataset dated April 27, 2017) of US patients still ill six or more months after antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease. It covers only rates of diagnostic delay, clinician-seeking before diagnosis, misdiagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia/psychiatric conditions, and self-identified disability. It does not model or include any dollar costs, caregiving hours, treatment effectiveness (which showed no significant sex difference in this document), or national prevalence - the document itself reports no cost data. Findings are associational, self-reported, and not generalizable beyond this registry sample.

takeaway.patient: In this patient registry, women were more likely than men to wait 3+ years for a Lyme disease diagnosis, to see 10 or more clinicians before being diagnosed, and to be told along the way that their symptoms were chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition instead. Women were also somewhat more likely to report being disabled from work because of Lyme disease. These are patterns reported by patients themselves in one self-selected online registry, not a guarantee of any individual's experience, but they may validate what many patients - especially women - have gone through before getting a correct diagnosis.
takeaway.care: Among persistent Lyme disease patients in this registry, women showed significantly higher rates of prolonged pre-diagnosis delay, higher numbers of clinicians consulted before diagnosis, and more frequent misattribution of symptoms to chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric illness, compared to men. Self-identified work disability was also somewhat higher among women. These sex-stratified patterns may be useful for differential-diagnosis awareness in patients presenting with ambiguous multisystem symptoms, though the data are self-reported and not chart-confirmed.
takeaway.policy: This registry-based study found statistically significant sex disparities favoring worse outcomes for women across diagnostic delay, clinician-visit burden, and misdiagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia/psychiatric conditions, alongside a smaller but significant disability gap. The document separately notes that NIH-funded RCT/post-treatment Lyme disease studies have historically excluded 89-99% of prospective enrollees through restrictive entry criteria, and that few trials were designed to examine sex as a variable at all. No cost or national burden estimate can be derived from this document.

patient: If you were previously diagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition before your Lyme disease diagnosis, consider raising with your clinician whether that earlier diagnosis should be revisited now.
If your diagnosis took years or involved many different clinicians, consider keeping a written symptom and visit timeline to share with any new provider to shorten future evaluations.
Ask your clinician whether testing for tick-borne coinfections was done, since this registry found coinfections were more commonly reported among women.

## Source and scope
All inputs and outputs come from a peer-reviewed study (IJGM 2023;16:2557-2566) analyzing the MyLymeData patient registry (n=2170 US residents with persistent/chronic Lyme disease, dataset dated April 27, 2017; 1839 women, 331 men). The document reports no dollar costs anywhere, so this simulator models only self-reported percentage rates and the percentage-point gaps between women and men for diagnostic delay, clinician-visit burden before diagnosis, misdiagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia/psychiatric conditions, and self-identified work disability. All four underlying comparisons are statistically significant in the document (p-values 0.030 to <0.0001).

## Limitations
**Claims-based undercounting**: the document cites a commonly referenced CDC estimate of 476,000 new Lyme disease diagnoses per year in the USA, derived from commercial insurance claims data (Schwartz et al. 2021) rather than symptom-based surveillance; such claims-derived counts likely undercount the true frequency of Lyme disease, since they miss undiagnosed, untreated, or non-claims-captured cases. This estimate is cited for context only and is not used in any calculation here.

**Subgroup disaggregation**: every figure modeled here is disaggregated by sex only. The study authors state their sample lacked sufficient diversity to examine variation by race/ethnicity or gender-spectrum identity, and the document provides no breakdown by age or other subgroups. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it.

**Systemic evidence-generation gap**: the document reports that NIH-funded randomized/post-treatment Lyme disease studies historically used entry criteria that excluded 89-99% of prospective enrollees, and that none of the NIH trials and very few other clinical studies were designed to examine sex differences as part of their research design - a gap in how persistent Lyme disease evidence itself gets generated, separate from the accuracy of any single estimate.

## Other cautions
All measures are self-reported by a self-selected, higher-income/education-skewed registry population, with no external chart confirmation. The document found no statistically significant sex difference in antibiotic treatment effectiveness, side effects, or self-rated fair/poor health, and those measures are not modeled here. Ranges on all inputs (0-100%) are an assumed exploration bound for this simulator, not a range specified in the source document.
